Citation These Regulations may be cited as the National Cereals and Produce Board Regulations, 1989, and shall be deemed to have come into operation on the 26th March, 1989. PART II – APPOINTMENT OF AGENTS 2. Certificate of appointment (1) Every agent appointed by the Board under section 12 of the Act shall be issued with a certificate of appointment which shall be in Form A set out in the Schedule. (2) The Board may from time to time attach conditions or additional conditions to the appointment of any person as an agent under section 12 of the Act or delete conditions therefrom and may enter the same in the certificate of appointment issued under paragraph (1). (3) For the purpose of making an entry under paragraph (2) or for the purpose of cancelling the certificate when the appointment has been revoked, the Board may, by notice in writing, require the holder of a certificate of appointment within a specified reasonable time to surrender the certificate to the Board for the entry to be made thereon, or for cancellation, as the case may be. (4) Any person

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: in writing, require the holder of a certificate of appointment within a specified reasonable time to surrender the certificate to the Board for the entry to be made thereon, or for cancellation, as the case may be. (4) Any person who without reasonable excuse fails to surrender a certificate of appointment when required to do so under paragraph (3) within the time allowed shall be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand shillings. PART III – CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION OF MILLERS 3. Conditions for registration The limitations and conditions subject to which a person may be registered as a miller under section 19(3) of the Act shall be— (a) that he shall purchase all his maize, wheat or agricultural produce from the Board or from persons authorized by the Board; (aa) that he shall collect any maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce purchased from the Board from the nearest depot of the Board or such collection centres as may be specified by the Board; (b) that he will, if so required by the Board— (i) store on behalf of the Board or its agents any quantity of maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce up to the capacity of his storage accommodation, at such remuneration as the Board may determine; (ii) on behalf of the

text: (i) store on behalf of the Board or its agents any quantity of maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce up to the capacity of his storage accommodation, at such remuneration as the Board may determine; (ii) on behalf of the Board or its agents store any maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce in such mixtures and quantities, and at such times, as the Board may direct, and at such remuneration as the Board may determine; (iii) deal with and dispose of the maize, wheat and scheduled agricultural produce which are the property of the Board in such manner as the Board may direct;

[L.N. 220/1989.] 4. Registered millers to keep records (1) Every miller registered under section 19(3) of the Act, shall maintain adequate records of all purchases, acquisitions, millings, sales and disposals by him of maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce and shall retain for a period of five years, so as to be available for inspection or production at all reasonable times, all accounts, books, documents, registers, invoices and cash sales relating to such transactions. (2) All records required to be kept under paragraph (1) shall be made in such a way as to distinguish between dealings with maize, wheat and scheduled agricultural produce and dealings with other goods. text: produce and dealings with other goods. PART IV – IMPORT AND EXPORT 5. Authority for import or export (1) The written authority without which, by virtue of subsection (1) of section 18 of the Act, no person may import or export any maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce shall be in the permit in Form B set out in the schedule or of a permit in form C set out in the Schedule, as the case may be. (2) Every person requiring the authority to export or import maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce shall make application therefore in Form D or E set out in the Schedule, as the case may require. (3) The fees payable on the issue or renewal of an import or export permit shall be 10 per cent of the declared C & F value or 10 per cent of the FOB value respectively. [L.N. 220/1989, L.N. 274/1989, L.N. 277/1990.] 6. Imported maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce subject to regulations Where any maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce have been imported into Kenya the same shall be subject to these Regulations to the same extent as if they have been produced in Kenya. 7. Maize, etc. in transit through Kenya (1) Every person requiring authority to import maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce for

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: same shall be subject to these Regulations to the same extent as if they have been produced in Kenya. 7. Maize, etc. in transit through Kenya (1) Every person requiring authority to import maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce for the purpose only of immediately exporting the same shall make application to the Board in Form F set out in the Schedule. (2) Every authority issued pursuant to paragraph (1) shall be in Form G set out in the Schedule and shall be issued subject to the directions issued by the Board that the maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce shall be exported within the stipulated time. PART V – RETURNS, REPORTS AND ESTIMATES 8. Returns by producers, etc. Every producer, distributor and retailer shall, when required by the Board render to the Board such returns, reports and estimates and shall thereafter supply such further particulars as may be required either by specific direction or by a subsequent request by the Board.

Returns by licensed millers (1) A licensed miller to whom an allocation of maize or wheat has been made under section 22 of the Act shall, within seven days of each month, submit to the Board a return containing the following particulars— (a) the number of bags of imported maize or wheat in stock as at the date of the return; (b) the number of bags of local maize or wheat in stock as at the date of the return; (c) the number of bags of wheat flour from imported and locally grown wheat in stock as at the date of the return; (d) the number of bags of maize flour from imported and locally grown maize in stock as at the date of the return; and (e) the number of bags or bales of imported maize or wheat flour in stock as at the date of the return. (2) The number of bags or bales of maize flour (locally processes or imported) sold during the month shall be recorded in Form H set out in the Schedule; and (3) The number of bags or bales of wheat flour (locally processed or imported) sold during the month shall be recorded in Form I set out in

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: month shall be recorded in Form H set out in the Schedule; and (3) The number of bags or bales of wheat flour (locally processed or imported) sold during the month shall be recorded in Form I set out in the Schedule. 10. Manner of dealing with maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce Every agent to whom maize, wheat or scheduled agricultural produce is delivered under the Act shall deal with the same in accordance with the conditions of his appointment. 11. Offence and general penalty Any person who contravenes the provisions of these Regulations shall be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding twenty thousand shillings or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years or to both. 12. Revocation The Maize Marketing Regulations made under the Maize Marketing Act (now repealed) and the Wheat Industry (Imports and Exports) Rules made under the Wheat Industry Act (now repealed) are revoked. text: [Rev. 2012] CAP. 338 National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] 49 [Issue 1] NATIONAL CEREALS AND PRODUCE BOARD (GRADING OF WHEAT) REGULATIONS, 1989 [L.N. 214/1989, L.N. 363/1989.] 1. (1) These Regulations may be cited as the National Cereals and Produce Board (Grading of Wheat) Regulations, 1989 and shall come into operation on the 1st July, 1989. (2) These Regulations shall apply to specifications and the method of sampling and determining grades of wheat grain belonging to the species Triticum aestivum and Triticum durum which are purchased for human consumption in Kenya. 2. (1) In these Regulations, unless the context otherwise requires— “broken grains” means shrivelled grains and pieces of wheat grain that will pass readily through a sieve in the manner described in the Seventh Schedule; “Datura” means that the seeds of the plant Datura stramonium: “foreign matter” means any material which is not wheat grain or fragments of wheat grains other than noxious weed seeds, earth, sand and stones; “grader” means a person in possession of a valid wheat grader’s certificate issue by the Kenya Bureau of Standards; “noxious weed” means any weed gazetted under the Suppression of ‘Noxious Weeds Act (Cap. 325); “reject wheat” means wheat which is or has been mouldly, musty or otherwise commercially objectionable, being unfit for human consumption; “shrievelled grain” means grain which is

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: weed” means any weed gazetted under the Suppression of ‘Noxious Weeds Act (Cap. 325); “reject wheat” means wheat which is or has been mouldly, musty or otherwise commercially objectionable, being unfit for human consumption; “shrievelled grain” means grain which is undeveloped, thin and papery in appearance; “treated wheat” means wheat which has been treated in such manner that the true quality is not reflected or has made the grain unfit for human consumption; “undergrade wheat” means wheat which can be brought back into grade; “wheat group” means wheat varieties which have been approved suitable to bulk or store together because of their similar baking characteristics as approved by the National Plant Breeding Station at Njoro. (2) For the purposes of these Regulations, the following shall be considered to be defective grains— (a) “germinated wheat”, that is, wheat in which the pericarp covering the embryo has been ruptured; (b) “infested wheat”, that is wheat grains containing in or amongst the grain any form of living insect, mite or other organism known to be capable of causing damage or spoilage to the grain; (c) “insect damaged wheat”, that is, wheat grains which have been damaged by any insect or any other pest; (d) “immature wheat”, that is, wheat which is not fully developed and the grains of which are distinctly green in

text: grain; (c) “insect damaged wheat”, that is, wheat grains which have been damaged by any insect or any other pest; (d) “immature wheat”, that is, wheat which is not fully developed and the grains of which are distinctly green in colour;

text: CAP. 338 [Rev. 2012] National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] [Issue 1] 50 (e) “heat damaged wheat” that is, wheat damaged by applied external heat or as a result of natural heating caused by fermentation due to initial high moisture as described in the Tenth Schedule; and (f) “weather damaged wheat” that is wheat grain of which one-third or more of its dorsal surface is damaged as described in the Tenth Schedule. 3. (1) Wheat grains shall have a moisture content of not more than 14.4 per cent calculated on the total mass of a sample of wheat grain as determined according to the Sixth Schedule. (2) The maximum permitted physical defects in all grades of wheat grain shall be as shown in the following Table 1. (b) Undergrade wheat in relation to Fair Average Quality wheat shall mean wheat which does not meet the requirements of Table 1 and is not reject. [L.N. 363/1989, r 2(c).] 5. Wheat samples shall be drawn by appointed graders at point of sale unless otherwise agreed in accordance with the procedures described in the Ninth Schedule. 6. The following instruments, equipment and methods shall be used for the purposes of grading wheat in accordance with the provisions of these Regulations— (a) the sampling of wheat grains in bags shall be carried out in the manner provided for in the First Schedule; (b) the sampling of wheat grains in bulk shall be carried out in the manner provided for in the Second Schedule; (c) the mechanical sample divider shall conform to the provisions of the Third Schedule; (d) the dividing of samples which have been mixed and evenly spread over a flat surface or “quartering” shall be in accordance with the Fourth Schedule; (e) the apparatus to be used for the determination of grade mass from a sample shall conform to the specifications set out in the Fifth Schedule; (f) the apparatus to be used for the determination of moisture shall conform to the specifications set out in the Sixth Schedule; (g) the method for determining the percentage of broken grains shall be as set out in the Seventh Schedule; (h) the weighing instrument for determining the mass of wheat grains contained in a measure shall be as set out in the Eighth Schedule; (i) the grading of samples shall be

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: CAP. 338 [Rev. 2012] National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] [Issue 1] 52 FIRST SCHEDULE [Rule 6(a).] SAMPLING OF WHEAT GRAINS IN BAGS 1. The standard sack sampler shall be a tapered steel tube capable of drawing representative samples when inserted through a gunny bag filled with wheat grains, and of a type approved by the Kenya Bureau of Standards. 2. Primary samples shall be drawn from different parts of the bag (for example, top, middle and bottom) by means of a standard sack sampler. The sampler shall be put into each sack towards the centre and to the full extent on the inverted slotted opening and then turned through 180 degrees. The sample shall then be withdrawn and the contents emptied into a container. The quantity of the grading sample drawn from a specific consignment shall not be less than two litres in volume. The contents of any bag which differs in any respect from this sample, shall be graded separately. SECOND SCHEDULE [Rule 6(b).] SAMPLING OF WHEAT GRAINS IN BULK 1. A bulk sampler shall be a type of device capable of drawing a representative sample from a bulk wagon, lorry or moving stream of wheat grains, and be of a type approved by the Kenya Bureau of Standards. The method of obtaining samples from the above containers

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: of device capable of drawing a representative sample from a bulk wagon, lorry or moving stream of wheat grains, and be of a type approved by the Kenya Bureau of Standards. The method of obtaining samples from the above containers shall be as follows— (i) probe in the centre of the container; (ii) probe from 1 to 2 metres back from the door-post towards the end of the container and 60 cm from one side of the container; (iii) probe from 1 to 2 metres from the same end of the container and approximately 60 cm from the opposite side of the container as in (ii); (iv) probe same as in (ii) and (iii) except in opposite end and sides of the container; (v) a sample may ‘be taken after direct transfer or “drop-back”, or by binning run method at the time of loading, or unloading as mentioned above. 2. Each probed sample of the grain shall be examined for uniformity in respect of group odour, moisture content, weather damage, heat damage and infestation with insects or other pests. If all portions are found to be uniform they shall be composited into one sample representing the entire consignment. If any portion is found to differ in grades or in quality characteristics, further sampling shall be dune to establish the fractional

If any portion is found to differ in grades or in quality characteristics, further sampling shall be dune to establish the fractional part of the entire consignment that is different and the result shall be indicated.

text: [Rev. 2012] CAP. 338 National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] 53 [Issue 1] THIRD SCHEDULE [Rule 6(c).] MECHANICAL SAMPLE DIVIDER 1. The mechanical sample divider shall be the apparatus used for randomly dividing a sample of wheat grains into equal separate portions, and be of a type approved by the Kenya Bureau of Standards. 2. The usage of this apparatus shall be according to the manufacturers’ instructions. FOURTH SCHEDULE [Rule 6(d).] QUARTERING 1. The quartering apparatus is constructed of two pieces of rigid material measuring approximately 45 cm. x 3 cm. each. They are joined at their centres to intersect at right angles in one plane. 2. The sample shall be thoroughly mixed and spread evenly in layers over a flat surface and divided into four approximately equal quarters by placing the quartering apparatus over the sample. Two quarters situated diagonally across the dividing line shall be combined together to constitute the sample. Further operation of the quartering apparatus using the above method shall be done where the original quartered sample is too large. FIFTH SCHEDULE [Rule 4.] DETERMINATION OF GRADE MASS FROM THE SAMPLE 1. (1) The apparatus consists of four different pieces of equipment, as described below. If other apparatus to that described proves to be accurate in determining grade mass, then, with Kenya Bureau of Standards approval,

(5) The Stroker—Shall be a cylindrical piece of wood having a length of approximately 15 cm and diameter of approximately 2.5 cm. 2. All relevant provisions of the Weights and Measures Act (Cap. 513) and the Rules thereunder shall be applicable to the weighing instruments and the other apparatus described above. 3. (1) The metal measure shall be first filled to over-flowing capacity with the sample of wheat grain to be measured by using a scoop or other suitable means. The over-flowing measure of wheat grain shall then be transferred to the funnel with the slide previously closed. The measure shall be stood on a firm level surface free from any vibration. The funnel containing the sample shall be placed on top of the measure. The slide shall then be withdrawn fully and smartly. After the funnel has been emptied it shall be removed from the measure without jarring the measure. The measure shall then be struck by placing the stroker horizontally on the edge of the measure and sweeping it across the top in one light semi-circular movement. title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: [Rev. 2012] CAP. 338 National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] 55 [Issue 1] SEVENTH SCHEDULE [Rule 6(g).] THE SIEVE AND ‘METHOD FOR DETERMINING PERCENTAGE OF BROKEN GRAINS 1. Apparatus—the sieve shall measure internally approximately 25 cm square by 5 cm. deep. The sieve shall be perforated with slots 1.6 mm wide and 9.5 mm long. In use it shall be fitted to a catch-box below and with a suitable lid on top to avoid spillage of any fraction being tested. 2. Description of the Sieving Test.—(1) A sample shall be made up of half a litre wheat grain already weighed for the hectolitre mass test which shall be used for determining shrivelled and broken grain. (2) The sieve shall be held level in both hands directly in front of the body with the elbows close to the sides. It shall be held so that the grain moves lengthwise with the perforation. The sieve shall be moved approximately 25 cm from right to left and returned from left to right to complete an operation, while maintaining the horizontal place. (3) The complete operation. shall be repeated thirty times at the above rate and the shaking shall continue for approximately 15 seconds, after which the sieve shall be given two taps on the side of the box to clear the perforations. (4)

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: complete operation. shall be repeated thirty times at the above rate and the shaking shall continue for approximately 15 seconds, after which the sieve shall be given two taps on the side of the box to clear the perforations. (4) The broken grains, as defined under regulation 2(1) which have passed through the screen and are found in the sieve box, shall be weighed. This mass divided by the original mass of the half litre of grain and multiplied by 100. shall be reported as the “percentage of broken grains”. EIGHTH SCHEDULE [Rule 6(h).] WEIGHING BALANCES 1. The weighing instrument used for determining the mass of wheat grains containing in the measure shall be of a self-indicating pattern which is acceptable by the Weights and Measures Department and the Kenya Bureau of Standards. For the purposes of assizing and stamping, the chart of the weighing instrument shall be graduated to a weighing capacity of 500 grams by 5 grams subdivisions, which shall be less than 2 mm apart. The weighing instrument shall be provided with a detachable goods pan in the form of a scoop. 2. The balance for assessing defects in wheat grain, as set out in Tables 1 and 2, shall have a capacity of 50 grams, with a minimum accuracy of 0.1 gram and of a type

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: the form of a scoop. 2. The balance for assessing defects in wheat grain, as set out in Tables 1 and 2, shall have a capacity of 50 grams, with a minimum accuracy of 0.1 gram and of a type approved by the Kenya Bureau of Standards. 3. All relevant provisions of the Weights and Measures Act (Cap. 513)and the rules made thereunder, shall apply to the weighing instruments. NINTH SCHEDULE [Rule 5 and 6(i).] GRADING SAMPLE 1. The grading sample, with a minimum volume of 2 litres, shall be obtained as set in the First and Second Schedules.

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: CAP. 338 [Rev. 2012] National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] [Issue 1] 56 2. (1) The sequence of determining factors to reach the final wheat grade, shall be as follows— (a) infested wheat; (b) moisture content; (c) quartering method—retain two quarters separately for analysis; (d) use first quarter to determine the following— (i) grade maw; (ii) broken grains; (iii) datura; (e) express the results as a percentage of the grade mass. (2) Use the second quarter to repeat determination of grade mass. Then, weigh two samples of 25 grams each from this quarter— (i) Use the first of these samples to determine the following defects as set out below— (a) foreign matter; (b) earth, sand and stones; (c) heat damaged wheat; (d) germinated wheat; (e) insect-damaged wheat; (f) immature wheat; (g) mixed groups. (ii) The perecentage of these defects be determined by hand picking from the sample in the order above and separated from each other. The defective materials separated are then weighed to a tolerance of 0.1 gram and the defects calculated and expressed as a percentage of the total mass of the 25 gram sample. (iii) Use the second of these samples to determine weather damage percentage as set out in the Tenth Schedule. TENTH SCHEDULE [Rule 2 (2).] RECOGNITION OF WEATHER DAMAGED AND HEAT DAMAGED WHEAT 1.

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: total mass of the 25 gram sample. (iii) Use the second of these samples to determine weather damage percentage as set out in the Tenth Schedule. TENTH SCHEDULE [Rule 2 (2).] RECOGNITION OF WEATHER DAMAGED AND HEAT DAMAGED WHEAT 1. Weather Damaged Wheat.—Take the sample referred to in the Ninth Schedule and spread this out on a light-green tile. Examine every grain on its dorsal surface only (each grain has a ventral surface, sides and dorsal, or back, surface). Separate weather damaged grain consisting of the following types of discolouration, physical damage and mould infection, provided that 1/3 or more of the dorsal surface of the grain is affected. 2. Type of Discolouration— (i) Parts of the grain near the brush end are grey, greyish black or dark brown. (ii) Parts of the grain are distinctly yellow. (iii) Parts of the grain are orange red. Grains which are bleached or pale but otherwise sound are not considered to be discoloured. The condition known as black point, which is a brown, dark brown or almost black disc at the embryo end of the grain is not considered be discolouration due to weather damage.

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: [Rev. 2012] CAP. 338 National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] 57 [Issue 1] 3. Physical Damage— (i) Badly distorted grains (except shrivelled grain). (ii) Grains in which part of the seed coat covering the endosperm is actually torn or peeled off. (The condition in which the seed coat appears loose and often bubbly, but is not actually torn, must be considered to be physically damaged.) 4. Mould Infection— (i) Small separate black spots scattered over the surface of the grain due to leaf blight (pyronophera trichostome). (ii) Greyish black discolouration of the brush end of the grain due to black mould (Cladosporium herborum). (iii) Pinkish red areas due to scab (Fusarium graminearum). In cases where mould infection appears as spots on the grain, the total area in which the spots are spread shall be considered. 5. Heat Damage: Heat damaged wheat displays the following defects, odour, colour, texture and chemical change. (i) Odour.—A typical characteristic smell akin to that of roasted wheat. (ii) Colour.—The surface colour, depending on the extent of heat damage, varies from reddish brown to black. The endosperm colour is not normal white or opaque, but is brownish. (iii) Texture.—The affected grain is cut by a blade, or preferably by a grain cutter, and the cut surface may display a crumbly and brittle texture depending on the

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: endosperm colour is not normal white or opaque, but is brownish. (iii) Texture.—The affected grain is cut by a blade, or preferably by a grain cutter, and the cut surface may display a crumbly and brittle texture depending on the extent of heat damage. (iv) The protein and starch has been denatured and this can be verified through rheological tests.

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)
text: [Rev. 2012] CAP. 338 National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] 59 [Issue 1] NATIONAL CEREALS AND PRODUCE BOARD (IMPORTATION OF MAIZE) REGULATIONS, 1993 [L.N. 335/1993.] 1. These Regulations may be cited as the National Cereals and Produce Board (Importation of Maize) Regulations, 1993. 2. Notwithstanding the provisions of the National Cereals and Produce Board Regulations, 1989 (L.N. 131/1989), any person may import any quantity of maize. 3. Paragraph 2 of the National Cereals and Produce (Movement of Maize, Wheat and Scheduled Agricultural Produce) (Amendment) Regulations, 1992 (L.N. 80/1992), shall not apply to the movement of maize imported under Regulation 2.

text: [Rev. 2012] CAP. 338 National Cereals and Produce Board [Subsidiary] 61 [Issue 1] NATIONAL CEREALS AND PRODUCE BOARD (EXPORTATION OF MAIZE) REGULATIONS, 2008 [L.N. 123/2008.] 1. These Regulations may be cited as the National Cereals and Produce Board (Exportation of Maize) Regulations, 2008. 2. No person shall export any quantity of maize, with effect from the date of publication of these Regulations until such a time when these Regulations shall be amended or revoked.

title: National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338)

These Regulations may be cited as the National Cereals and Produce Board (Exportation of Maize Products) Regulations, 2008. 2. No person shall export any part or product of maize, whether or not it has been ground or sifted into flour or otherwise treated, to any country.

text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board vii EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 1 Introduction The National Cereals and Produce Board of Kenya (NCPB) is a corporate body established in 1985 under the National Cereals and Produce Board Act (Cap 338) of the laws of Kenya. It was formed by the amalgamation of The Maize and Produce Board and The Wheat Board on 1st July 1979. The merger was formalised in August 1985 through The NCPB Act (Cap 338). The Board was established by the Government to regulate and control the marketing and processing of grains in Kenya. This was to be achieved through licensing and regulating the key players in the sector, who include traders, farmers and millers. Other players in the sector include the government, transporters, non-governmental organisations, institutions and the public. The Board’s mandate includes: Commercial trading in grains; Provision of commodity handling and other grain related services including carrying out various social functions such as Strategic Grain Reserve and Famine Relief on behalf of the Government; Procuring and marketing high quality farm inputs; Provision of storage and grain maintenance services to clients; Provision of information on national and international grain trading. The objective of this study is to propose recommendations for restructuring of the NCPB in order to enhance its service delivery on a sustainable basis. 2 Rationale behind Restructuring NCPB The rationale behind restructuring NCPB is informed by decisions that can draw from: Lessons learnt from previous restructuring efforts, Challenges currently facing NCPB, and Lessons learnt from best practices both locally and internally. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 1 1 BACKGOUND OF THE STUDY 1.1 History and the Mandate of the NCPB National Cereals and Produce Board (NCPB) has a long history, which dates back 1939. It started as Maize and Produce Board formed to support marketing of grains produced by the colonial settlers both locally and internationally. In 1967, there was amalgamation of the Maize and Produce Marketing Board with all other regional marketing boards into the Maize and Produce Board. This was to consolidate the marketing of maize within the region after independence of the East African Nations. Later, the Maize and Produce Board merged with Wheat Board of Kenya thus putting the two major grains in the country under one umbrella. This was to ease the control of the cereal subsector. In 1985 the NCPB Act. Cap.338 was enacted creating the NCPB as a state monopoly charged with the mandate to control the procurement and distribution of maize, wheat and scheduled agricultural commodities. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 10 3.1.5 Key Challenges on Governance, Legal and Regulations Frameworks The Board’s key challenge as shared by majority of the stakeholders is its conflicted mandate. Is NCPB a commercial enterprise or a social enterprise? NCPB has been labelled as a commercial enterprise or a social enterprise at the convenience of the key players. The NCPB Act, the statute establishing NCPB, is now outdated and does not adequately address the current needs and objectives of NCPB. The Act is no longer responsive to the needs of NCPB as it was enacted when NCPB was a key social corporation for the government of Kenya. Compliance with the Public Procurement and Disposal Act (PPDA) deprives the NCPB of a competitive edge in the market place as other competing commercial enterprises are not bogged down by the bureaucratic procurement regulations. The NCPB Act has established the Board as a body corporate capable of suing and being sued. NCPB is that the Board is easily targeted for litigation, and some of the litigation has even questioned the mandate of the Board. These challenges call for repeal of the NCPB Act cap 338, in order to redefine NCPB as a commercial entity and provides for its powers, objections and functions in line with commercialization principles. 3.1.6 Grain

text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 12 3.2 Organisation Structure and Staffing 3.2.1 Organisation Structure NCPB has in place a hierarchical organizational structure which has evolved over the last 30 years since its establishment as a monopoly and regulator of maize and other agricultural produce. Hierarchical organizational structures exhibit a bureaucratic culture or “red tape” which stifles creativity and innovation and a tendency for employees to work towards the basic minimum productivity levels. The most significant change to the organizational structure was the creation of a functional divisional structure in 1996 after the liberalization of the maize sector in 1993 following implementation of the Cereal Sector Reform Programme undertaken by the Government of Kenya supported by the European Union, World Bank and the International Monetary Fund between 1988 and 1993. The transformation of NCPB into a commercial trading entity required a dramatic reorientation of its workforce from a bureaucratic culture to a customer focused and results driven commercial business culture, which has proved elusive. In 2009, NCPB developed a strategic plan (20092013) which clarified its mission and articulated a new vision on which the future trajectory of the organization will be based. Arising from the Strategic Plan, the Board approved a new organizational structure, which increased the number of functional divisions from 2 to 5. This was

title: NCPB Restructuring Report 2014 (cost of maize production)
text: articulated a new vision on which the future trajectory of the organization will be based. Arising from the Strategic Plan, the Board approved a new organizational structure, which increased the number of functional divisions from 2 to 5. This was achieved by splitting the Marketing function from the Operations docket to create the Commercial division and also splitting the Finance and Administration division to create the Human Resources and Administration division. A new division of “Commodity Exchange” (COMEX) was created to promote a trading platform with the aim of reducing operating costs along the value chain from producers and traders to processors and consumers for the benefit of the agricultural sector and the economy as a whole. In addition, it was proposed to establish a Warehouse Receipting System” (WRS) to strengthen the supply chain by creating an efficient handling and storage facility. However, it is important to note that this approved organization structure was never implemented and the organization continues to operate on the basis of the old structure. 3.2.1.1 Current High Level Organizational Structure NCPB’s current organisational structure is based on functional grouping of similar areas of activities. This structure is characterised by technical specialisation to facilitate easier managerial control. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 17 3.2.2 Analysis of Core Vs Non-Core Business Functions The functioning of NCPB can be broken down into two key functional areas namely: core functions revolving around grain storage and non-core functions. Core functions consist of the primary business activity which can never be outsourced. Core functions represent the core business activities of grain procurement, grading drying, cleaning, storage, quality and pest control as well as logistics and distribution. Other areas include quality assurance, technical maintenance as well as sales and marketing. 56.05% (570) of the staff are deployed in the core business functions. Support functions represent the non-core business activities of the organization to ensure proper support to the core function. Support functions are not directly related to operational activities and cover such services as public relations, legal services, finance, human resources, administration as well as information and communication technology. Professional services are knowledge-based, such as recruitment, training, procurement, budgeting and financial reporting which are essential and add value to the core activity. Professionals support services is considered “mission critical” and the goal is to provide high quality service at lower cost and more efficiently. On the other hand transactional services consist of repetitive and generic tasks such as secretarial, clerical, accounting, data entry, driving, cleaning and maintenance and security.

The SBU management principle is therefore an opportunity for NCPB to introduce an entrepreneurial culture and drive in all the 6 regions. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 26 3.3 Operations and Commercial Activities 3.3.1 Current business model The current Business Model comprises of the following main segments: Product / Service Lines: Commercial function (Commodities and farm inputs training and other grain related commercial services). Social function (GOK Stocks, i.e. strategic grain reserves, food relief, price support, GOK subsidy program and interventions). 3.3.1.1 Grain Products NCBP is involved in commercial trading in grains. The Board trade in maize, wheat, gunnies, beans, seeds, wimbi, green grams and paddy rice among others. The products currently being sold by the Board include branded and unbranded maize, rice and beans in various package sizes. The pricing of the above grain products is market-driven through flexible pricing structure that takes into account competition, customer needs and NCPB’s market share and profitability. 3.3.1.2 Firm Inputs The board is also involved in procuring and marketing high quality farm inputs including fertiliser and insecticides. The annual demand for fertilizer is estimated at 400,000 Metric Tons. The Board handles about 100,000 Metric Tons leaving the balance to be supplied by the private sector players. 3.3.1.3 Other Commercial services Further, the board also offer commodity handling/storage and maintenance services to clients especially farmers. With its depots and silos network spread across the country, the Board is also able to

text: supplied by the private sector players. 3.3.1.3 Other Commercial services Further, the board also offer commodity handling/storage and maintenance services to clients especially farmers. With its depots and silos network spread across the country, the Board is also able to offer warehousing facilities to farmers and traders at a fee. The board also markets its excess properties and services to generate income to sustain itself. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 27 3.3.1.4 Social activities of the Board In addition to the Board’s principal activities which include grain handling, marketing with provision of allied services and facilities, the Board’s social activities on behalf of the Government on Agency basis include procurement, storage, quality maintenance, and distribution /sale of famine relief food commodities as well as Strategic Grain Reserve stock. 3.3.2 Stakeholders’ Views on Commercial Activities Millers would want to see the Board stock maize from the farmers so that they pick the same from the nearest depot and this way avoid the many costs they incur looking for maize all over the country. They would also avoid the high commissions they pay to the maize brokers. The millers complained that they go to Board Depots to buy maize, they can see the maize stocked in the warehouses but they cannot buy because it is SGR Stocks and authority must be sought from Head Office or from the Ministry concerned. It was very apparent that most of these SGR stocks were acquired in 2008 / 2009 and have been deteriorating at a very high level due to attack by the weevils. The Board should be given authority to start selling this old stock and buy new stocks to replenish the old stock just

title: NCPB Restructuring Report 2014 (cost of maize production)
text: 2008 / 2009 and have been deteriorating at a very high level due to attack by the weevils. The Board should be given authority to start selling this old stock and buy new stocks to replenish the old stock just sold. This should be a continuous trading activity of the Board and the Depot Managers with proper controls and monitoring should be able to undertake this trading activity effectively. In order to deepen trading in maize and other commodities, it was suggested that the Board should package the maize and other products into smaller packages of 10 Kg, 20 Kg and 50 Kg bags, respectively order to appeal to small scale traders. This in our opinion was a good suggestion which the Board should embrace in order to be customer oriented and to meet the demands of the market. It became very clear from the stakeholders and the Board staff alike that Head Office must treat the regions as Profit Centers (Not Cost Centers). In view of this, Head Office should give region heads delegated authority to run as such. This would also call for rationalization of branch organization structures so that they can have qualified Accountants at Branch level to control and account for money collected from trade transactions and furnish Head Office with regular reports online on a

title: NCPB Restructuring Report 2014 (cost of maize production)
text: This would also call for rationalization of branch organization structures so that they can have qualified Accountants at Branch level to control and account for money collected from trade transactions and furnish Head Office with regular reports online on a 12 hours service. They may also have authority to invest excess funds in short term securities in the commercial banks where they are located with the approval of Head office. The commercial farmers were quite conversant and happy with the usage of Warehouse Receipts. The main challenge was the small scale farmers who argued that they were unable to get cash from banks particularly the Agricultural Financial Corporation (AFC) which never recognized the Warehouse Receipts due to lack of WRS legal framework. As soon the legal framework of the Warehouse Receipts legislated by the Government, Banks and other Financial Institutions should be able to embrace the Warehouse Receipts. Farmers complained that they travel long distances to secure allocation of subsidized fertilizers from the District Agricultural Officers and when they get allocations, they then have to travel further long distances to pay at the Board’s Banks and later get into long cures to secure the product they have paid for. The farmers urged that they should get fertilizers allocations ahead of the planting season so that they do not go rushing

title: NCPB Restructuring Report 2014 (cost of maize production)
text: pay at the Board’s Banks and later get into long cures to secure the product they have paid for. The farmers urged that they should get fertilizers allocations ahead of the planting season so that they do not go rushing the last minute. It was agreed that the farmers should organize themselves into groups since they seem to know each other, register the representatives with the Board and the Board will in turn be notifying these representatives in good time when commodities are going to become available. The Depots are ready and willing to deliver the fertilizers to designated centers located in the vicinity of various farmers’ groups. The Depots and even Head Office should sign agency arrangements with several Seed Companies and Suppliers of Herbicides on consignment basis to distribute them to the farmers as a One Stop Shop. This way the Board will be able to take the service closer to the farmers. But the Depots must also be properly and effectively facilitated by Head Office via reliable vehicles, other logistics and finances to operate.

IT management was involved during the strategy formulation, and this was facilitated with the help of Netcom Information Systems Limited consultants, who were charged with coming up with the strategy document. These applications were developed by the vendor and customized for NCPB. Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS), General Packet Radio Service (GPRS) or Wimax to allow for real time processing of transactions connects the depots or silos. Hardware acquisitions are made based on the funds availed as opposed to being based on reliability, scalability and performance in the light of future IT and business requirements. There are backup procedures, which allow for the security of data. There is lack of disaster recovery plan and a business continuity plan. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 38 3.4.6 Financial Challenges Faced by NCPB 1. Lack of Adequate Working Capital Lack of adequate working capital negatively affects NCPB’s ability to undertake its commercial operations. The Board’s main causes of inadequate working capital are attributed to the following: The Board incurred a loss of Kshs. 2.2 billion in 2001/2012 which arose from selling of commercial maize through Government directive. Delay in settlement of 2001/2002 export loss of Kshs. 2.2 billion by Government which severely eroded the working capital. The same has not been settled to date; Delay by MOALF and MoSSP to pay for services rendered on due dates; Delay by MOALF to pay subsidies on time on fertilizer sold at subsidized rates resulting in holding loans for long; Inadequate budgetary provisions in printed estimates for SGR and Famine Relief; Failure by MOALF to pay agency fees at commercial rates; NCPB being made to operate depots that are not commercially viable; Failure by MoPD to pay full cost of operating depots maintained for relief operations. 2. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 39 3.5 Grain Market and Policy Issues The grain sector in Kenya consists of the cereals and the pulses sub-sectors. 3.5.1 Cereal Sub-Sector The most important cereal crops grown in Kenya include maize, wheat and rice that are under the mandate of NCPB. Other grain crops grown in the country consist of sorghums, millets, barley and rye. 3.5.1.1 Maize Maize is the major staple food in Kenya. About 90 percent of Kenya’s population depends on maize as an income-generating commodity and food. Production has not kept pace with demand, which is mainly driven by the expanding population implying that the country has had to depend on imports (cross-border and off-shore) to bridge its production/consumption gaps. It is estimated that maize imports have averaged 15 percent of total consumption since 1996. However, the share of maize imports is highly understated because of massive unreported cross border trade from Uganda and Tanzania. Suffice to say at this point that maize forms the bulk of NCPB business and accounts for over 60 percent of its business turn-over. Whereas the tenets of liberalization dictate that maize prices be market driven, in Kenya government directives on prices to be applied by NCPB have distorted the functionality of markets and the Board’s profitability. 3.5.1.2 Wheat Wheat is

title: NCPB Restructuring Report 2014 (cost of maize production)
text: its business turn-over. Whereas the tenets of liberalization dictate that maize prices be market driven, in Kenya government directives on prices to be applied by NCPB have distorted the functionality of markets and the Board’s profitability. 3.5.1.2 Wheat Wheat is the second, most important cereal crop in Kenya after maize. Currently the country imports up to 70 percent of its wheat requirements. Unlike maize where NCPB has a great interest, the marketing of wheat has been liberalized. Through the Cereal Growers Association (CGA), a producer organization, wheat farmers have an agreement with millers that guarantees that millers purchase all domestically produced wheat before commencing imports. 3.5.1.3 Rice Rice is mainly consumed in urban areas. National production over the past two decades has varied between 38,000 metric tons and 53,000 metric tonnes. These schemes account for about 95 percent of total domestic production. The remaining 5 percent of the rice is rain-fed and is grown mainly along the coastal and riverine regions. The government has recently embarked on a rainfed rice production scheme in Western Kenya that is expected to reverse the current production situation. The annual consumption is estimated at 135,000 metric tonnes, implying that over 60 percent of the national consumption requirement is imported mainly from Pakistan, Thailand and Vietnam. NCPB actively participates in the marketing of rice and

text: the current production situation. The annual consumption is estimated at 135,000 metric tonnes, implying that over 60 percent of the national consumption requirement is imported mainly from Pakistan, Thailand and Vietnam. NCPB actively participates in the marketing of rice and unlike maize paddy prices are driven by the markets forces. 3.5.1.4 Pulse Sub-Sector The production of pulses in Kenya, which consist mainly of beans, green grams, cowpeas, pigeon peas and soya beans, has been playing a secondary role to maize production. Beans for example are intercropped with maize, and hardly receive attention in the same way that maize does in terms of the use of inputs and crop husbandry. There are many varieties of pulses grown in the country depending on the communities that consume them and the suitability of weather conditions in any given region. Pulses are mainly consumed together with cereals in most meals. The most important pulses for NCPB include beans and green grams. 3.5.2 Current Policy Framework Through a series of economic measures in 1980s and 1990s, the grain industry was first liberalized in 1993 and the Board finally commercialized with effect from July 1997.

text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 40 The Board has operated under an obsolete legal and regulatory framework since the commencement of commercialization. The NCPB Act, Cap 338 of Laws of Kenya, established the Board as purely a regulatory body with the mandate of regulating and controlling the movement and marketing of maize, wheat and scheduled produce. The legal framework became irrelevant with commercialization. In this regard, the Board, working with the parent Ministry of Agriculture and Office of the President, Special Programmes and other stakeholders has pushed for the enactment of the NCPC Bill, 2006 to establish the National Cereals and Produce Corporation, a corporate body. The Bill provides for the commercial mandate as well as advisory role and desirable intervention through participation as an agent of the Government. However, the bill is yet to be enacted. 3.5.3 Keys Players in the Cereals Market The grains subsector in Kenya is organised into different actors that play regulatory, research, production, trade, transportation and value addition functions. NCPB is the major grain dealer in Kenya and has over 50 years of experience in this sub-sector. Its activities were performed on monopoly basis until 1993 when the cereal sub-sector was liberalized. The advent of liberalization brought on board other players in the grain market that were non-existent during the

text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 42 3.5.3.1 Government (Ministries and other Departments) The Government has a responsibility of ensuring that every Kenyan is food secure. The government has delegated this responsibility to NCPB, which is expected to maintain the country’s strategic grain reserve stock, undertake distribution of relief supplies and intervene in the market during periods of adverse conditions. The Government allocates funds to NCPB to undertake these functions on Agency basis. The Government, through the Ministry of Agriculture, formulates grain sector policies, offers extension services and scrutinizes the activities of NCPB in order to safeguard the country’s food security position. Other key government agencies include the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute (KARI) and the Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS) that are engaged in research and seed regulation respectively. 3.5.3.2 Seed and agro-input dealers The major agro-input dealers include seed and fertilizer stockists who are distributors of seed and fertilizer companies respectively (Figure 1). Currently, the country has about 8 major seed production and marketing companies supplying seed to the domestic and regional export market. Besides the seed companies, KARI, CIMMYT and some NGO’s and CBO’s also supply certified seed maize. On the other hand there are about seven major fertilizer marketing companies and a multiple of agro-stockists. NCPB continues to market seed maize for Kenya

title: NCPB Restructuring Report 2014 (cost of maize production)
text: the seed companies, KARI, CIMMYT and some NGO’s and CBO’s also supply certified seed maize. On the other hand there are about seven major fertilizer marketing companies and a multiple of agro-stockists. NCPB continues to market seed maize for Kenya seed, the dominant seed company in Kenya and has recently diversified to fertilizer importation and distribution. NCPB also distributes fertilizer on agency basis for two of the country’s fertilizer manufacturers; Athi River Mining and KEL Chemicals. 3.5.3.3 Farmers Farmers are the sole providers of commodities that NCPB deals with. The farmers’ activities are therefore very critical to the existence of NCPB. Based on key subsector observers, average maize production in the last five years was about 31 million bags. Of this total smallholder farmers accounted for about 70 percent while medium to large farmers accounted for the rest. According to key respondents (NCPB, farmers and traders), smallholder farmers retain approximately 20-30 percent of their production for household consumption depending on perceived supply situation (Figure 1). They sell the balance 70-80 percent for cash-though a significant number of household also re-purchase stocks from the market during the last half of the crop year. About 25 percent of this marketable surplus is normally traded by and through NCPB. This implies that the level of NCPB’s activity is directly dependent on the level

This implies that the level of NCPB’s activity is directly dependent on the level of activity of farmers, holding all the other factors constant. 3.5.3.4 Millers and other Grain Traders At the marketing level, small-scale traders, medium to large traders, animal feed processors and NCPB are major players. Small scale traders handle 15-20% of total marketed production. Medium-large traders and their agents handle between 30 and 40% of total marketed production, while NCPB is estimated to be handling 25-30%. Millers handle about 25% total marketed volume. This category of stakeholders presents the greatest competition to the activities of NCPB and influences the way NCPB conducts its business. NCPB is the largest grain trader in Kenya. NCPB competes with millers and other traders in the grain market and the quantities realized are dependent on the flexibility and the ease with which each market entrant interacts with farmers, not to mention the promptness in payment. Kenya has 22 millers categorized into 18 large capacity millers (150 tons/24 hours) and 4 medium scale millers (50 – 150 tons/24 hours). The country’s installed milling capacity is about 3,500 tons/day although a majority of this capacity is underutilized. The

On the average it costs about Kshs 6,700 to prepare land in addition to another Kshs 4,000 where land is leased. The cost of land preparation alone accounts for 20 percent of the total cost of production. This cost can be substantially reduced if farmers adopted more innovative techniques of land preparation such as zero tillage whose cost is estimated to be a third of the conventional cost of land preparation. The key constraints to the sectors performance include; low farm productivity, constrained market access by smallholder grain farmers, lack of regional trade intelligence and market information; lack of a structured grain trade in the region, underutilization of installed milling capacity, high and increasing costs of processing, limiting and weak trade policy environments and lack of institutional frameworks and arrangement for structured trading in grain. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 46 4 PROPOSED RESTRUCTURING PROCESS 4.1 Rationale behind the Restructuring the NCPB The rationale behind restructuring NCPB is informed by decisions that can draw from: Lessons learnt from previous restructuring efforts, Challenges currently facing NCPB, and Lessons learnt from best practices both locally and internally. 4.1.1 Lessons learnt from previous restructuring efforts The previous reform initiatives aimed at streamlining the grain sector and transforming NCPB into a commercially viable organisation. It is worth noting that previous reforms aimed at making NCBP a commercial organisation, but the Board was still to perform the two main functions for the GOK namely SGR/FRS function and grain market stabilisation role, here referred as social functions. Why the Social functions? Though NCPB is categorized as a commercial entity, the board undertakes social functions on behalf of the Government on Agency basis. The agency agreement requires the Government avail funds to NCPB upfront to meet direct costs, fees and charges payable based on pre-costing of activities to be undertaken. Despite the Agency agreement the GOK has been delaying to pay for services rendered on due dates; provides inadequate budgetary provisions for SGR and Famine Relief and does not pay agency fees at commercial rates. In addition, the fixing of price payable to farmers for SGR at harvest

title: NCPB Restructuring Report 2014 (cost of maize production)
text: delaying to pay for services rendered on due dates; provides inadequate budgetary provisions for SGR and Famine Relief and does not pay agency fees at commercial rates. In addition, the fixing of price payable to farmers for SGR at harvest time makes NCPB uncompetitive in the market resulting in millers buying directly from farmers or from private maize traders, which effecting NCPB capacity to purchase its commercial stocks. The result is low margins in commercial sales and high stock holding costs. Consequently undertaking Strategic Grain Reserve and Famine Relief on behalf of the Government will remain as “social functions” to NCPB as there are not provided in arm length manner. From the previous reform initiatives, we also learn that; The grain sector has been operating without an independent regulator. This creates a void in the regulation of the sector giving the government a free hand to directly influence the sector and the operations of the Board. The mandate of NCPB is overlapping: It plays grain market stabilisation, commercial and social functions. Finally, failure to implement or fully implement the previous restructuring recommendations explains the current challenges facing NCPB. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 48 4.1.4 Elements of Restructuring Process There is an overlap in the current mandates of NCPB: It plays grain market stabilisation, commercial and social functions. Thus, it is not possible to restructure NCPB without having an insight of the entire grain sector. Lessons from previous NCPB restructuring efforts tells us that it is not visible to transform NCPB to commercial viable entity while it still undertaking social function. Consequently, the Business model current used by the NCPB is not commercial viable. The question is “in a liberalised and free economy is it possible for a Government parastatal to be commercially viable while still playing such social functions on an non-arm’s length basis?” There is need therefore to separate, NCPB commercial and social functions. Consequently, it is appropriate and suitable to separate NCPB functions. This will involve transferring some of the functions to other appropriate entities or create suitable entities that will effectively undertake them. We therefore recommended the following; I. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 50 5 GRAIN SECTOR REGULATOR 5.1 Introduction There is no market without a regulator. The Capital Markets Authority (CMA) is the regulator for Nairobi Security Exchange. The Central Bank is the regulator for the Banking Industry. The Communication Commission of Kenya (CCK) is the regular for telecommunication service providers, while the Energy Commission of Kenya (ECK) is the regulator for the Energy sector. Before the liberalization of the grain sector in 1993, NCPB had monopoly powers and was empowered to regulate and control the procurement, processing, sale, distribution, importation and exportation of maize, wheat and other scheduled produce. Commercialisation of NCPB created a void in the regulation and enforcement of policies. However, after liberalization in 1993 the Government through the Ministry of Agriculture has played a partial role in regulating the grain market but there is need for a more focused market regulation to ensure a fair orderly and efficient market. In view of this, it is suggested that the Government establishes a “Grain Sector Regulator” (GSR) to fall under the purview of the MoALF. While the Ministry will be deal with grain sector policy formulation the regulator will deal with policy implementation and enforcement. 5.2 Functions of GSR Support a competitive and efficient grain sector Maintain market integrity, fair, orderly,

The players include commodity exchange market, warehouse receipting operator and other market players Ensure (enforce) compliance with relevant standards, rules and regulations that will govern the grain sector The GSR will promote the self-regulatory in the sector. Here the GSR will be concerned primarily with promoting the disclosure of important market-related information, maintaining fair dealing, and protecting against fraud. One of the major sources of information on which the GSR will rely on is to bring enforcement action is market players themselves — educated and careful market players are so critical to the functioning of an efficient grain market. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 52 6 NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY AGENCY 6.1 Introduction The government supports the procurement and storage of Strategic Grain Reserves (SGR) to guarantee availability of grain in situations of extreme drought and famine and also to contribute to the stabilization of market prices in order to protect the poor and prevent market failure. The most critical challenge facing NCPB is the management and operation of the SGR on behalf of the government on Agency basis and the delays encountered in receiving payment for maintaining the reserve. We recommended that the Government to fundamentally move away from directly dealing with maize in the form of SGR. It is not viable and sustainable to store physical SGR for more than 5 years. First, the reserve will be go bad and second it is very costly for the Government to maintain the reserve, already the Government has spent billions of shillings maintaining the reserve. The best practise to allow the NCPB to continue trading the maize and other grains and the government will monitor the reserve to ensure that at any point in time the Board and other players has at least the required minimum reserve in existing storage facilities. Ideally, the food and grain reserve is monitored through a well-functioning warehouse receipting and commodity

Ideally, the food and grain reserve is monitored through a well-functioning warehouse receipting and commodity exchange systems. This is the case in South Africa and other developed/developing nations like Australia where they do not maintain any physical reserve. Similarly, USA manages food security by monitoring food in the warehouses mainly private silo operators. When the Government gets warning signals about impending food shortage, it buys all the grains in the private warehouses / silos and gets issued with silo certificates. This triggers the private grain dealers via exchange to import maize from outside to build stocks. However, in absence of a well functioning warehousing receipting and exchange, institutionalisation of food security and management is increasingly becoming norm for most developed and developing countries who have been establishing national food security agencies. However, it will take time to establish the COMEX, warehousing operators and create the requisite legal and regulatory framework as well as institutional frameworks that will enable monitoring of food reserve. The chairman who is nonexecutive is appointed by the President. However, all other members of the Board including the Managing Director/Chief Executive are appointed by the Cabinet Secretary for Agriculture. All appointments are for a period of three years, unless specified otherwise. The Board has been strengthened significantly by providing a mix of independent Directors and public officers to ensure a balance of skills and experience appropriate for the requirements of the business. However, the recently appointed taskforce on parastatal reforms has intimated that the State Corporations Act, Cap 446 will be revised to cater for better corporate governance in line with best practices. We recommend that the composition and skill set of a Board should depend on the GCK’s strategic vision and particular challenges encountered in the wider grain sector. An ideal Board for a commercially oriented organization should comprises a mix of knowledge and expertise in: accounting and finance; risk management; strategic and business planning; legal and compliance; human resources; marketing; international trade; and industry-specific research and development (R&D). The warehousing legislation must meet several conditions which include; Warehouse receipts must be functionally equivalent to stored commodities; The rights, liabilities, and duties of each party to a warehouse receipt (for example a farmer, a bank, or a warehouse) must be clearly defined; Warehouse receipts must be freely transferable by delivery and endorsement; The holder of a warehouse receipt must be first in line to receive the stored commodity or their fungible equivalent on liquidation or default of the warehouse;

As a result support functions within many organizations are undergoing fundamental change as a result of new technologies, changing skills demand and increased pressures to reduce costs and sustain long term competitive advantage. It is therefore critical to determine the right mix of professional, technical and supporting staff required for efficient and effective business operations. Support functions represent the non-core business activities of the organization to ensure proper support to the core function. Support functions are not directly related to operational activities and cover such services as public relations, legal services, finance, human resources, administration as well as information and communication technology. Professional services are knowledge-based, such as recruitment, training, procurement, budgeting and financial reporting which are essential and add value to the core activity. Professionals support services is considered “mission critical” and the goal is to provide high quality service at lower cost and more efficiently. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 102 Other risks associated with proposed restructuring model NCPB is exposed to a variety of risk as a result of the activities that it is engaged into. Risk Management Function is therefore important to manage enterprise-wide risk to cushion the organization from losses that may arise from normal operations as well other risks arising from the environment it operates in. Key risks to the organization regardless of the financing model that it adopts are as follows:- a) Political risk – This involves political, economic and social events that may result either collectively or individually to financial losses b) Economic risk – NCPB is engaged in transactions with businesses across various sectors such as Agriculture, Manufacturing, Transport, Energy etc. The financial prosperity is dependent on formulation of policy and procedures to support initiatives by both public and private sectors to remain profitable and yield financial returns. c) Regulatory risk – This relates to the risk of non-compliance or non-conformity with the laws, rules, regulations, prescribed practice or ethical standards issued from time to time. Drastic changes or new policy guidelines issued by regulatory bodies could im[pact on the financial performance of NCPB. d) Operational risk – This is the risk of direct or indirect loss arising from a wide variety of causes

These have been fully addressed in the report. As opposed to the current SGR trustees, NAFOSA will be institutionalized through an act of Parliament. The governing body will be a board and management will be constituted 2 The proposed Grain Sector Regulator of Kenya (GRCK) should create an enabling environment for structured trading in the grain subsector. (Yes, indeed the detailed functions of the GRCK are contained in the report) 3 The current government structure has placed the management of Strategic Grain Reserves (SGR) docket under the Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries (MOAFL) and the Famine Relief (FR) docket under the Ministry of Devolution and Planning (MODP). Currently the reconstitution of the SGR Trustees is ongoing. text: Study on Restructuring the National Cereals and Produce Board 139 Annex VII: Terms of Reference of the Study Background The National Cereals and Produce Board (NCPB) is a state owned corporation within the Ministry of Agriculture (MOA). It is located in Industrial Area, Nafaka House along Machakos Road. It is vested with the responsibility of carrying out commercial trading activities towards achieving Grain Price Stabilization, providing logistic support services for Strategic Grain Reserve (SGR) and Famine Relief Stocks (FRS) on agency basis. The Board is also involved in distribution of farm inputs and agro-chemicals to support grain production. The Government of Kenya seeking the services of a competent consultant to assist in the restructuring of the Board to enhance service delivery. To achieve the stated objective, MOA wishes to engage a qualified and experienced consultancy firm to execute the assignment on consultancy contract basis. The selected consultancy firm shall have a proven track record and extensive hands on experience in consultancy services relating to restructuring of institutions. The firm shall have a good knowledge and understanding in working with public owned institutions. Specifically, the firm MUST have successfully undertaken of at least four (4) assignments of similar nature in developing countries (Clients’ references will be required for this). The firm should have a minimum experience of at least three years

WHEREAS The Government of Kenya wishes to maintain a stock of maize and other food items for purposes of safeguarding National Food Security and wishes to hold these Strategic Grain Reserve Stocks in sound and high quality storage facilities and subject to modern grain management practices; The Government of Kenya wishes to maintain adequate capacity to intervene in Kenya’s grain and other food commodities deemed necessary for grain market stabilization purposes, either through purchasing from producers during periods of surplus production or through provision of supplies to the domestic market during periods of deficits; The Government of Kenya wishes to maintain adequate capacity and expertise to deliver/distribute grain supplies as and when needed; The Government of Kenya wishes to appoint National Cereals and Produce Board, a well established State Corporation with expertise in the procurement, storage, management and distribution of food commodities as an Agent in handling the above functions under the following terms and conditions. Article 2: Appointment of the Agent The Principal hereby appoints and the Agent agrees to be appointed as Agent to the Principal for purposes of the implementation of the Principal’s policies with respect to the National Strategic Grain Reserves, Stabilization of the Domestic Grain Market and implementation of intervention Programmes. Article 3: Description of the Services to be Performed by the Agent The services to be undertaken by the Agent shall include, but not limited to:-

Article 4: Obligations of the Agent 4.1 The Agent undertakes at all times to apply modern quality maintenance practices to all food and non food stocks of the Principal as defined in the preamble of this Agreement. It will in particular undertake necessary routine measures for: - Maintenance of grains within specified quality parameters To ensure that the annual grain shrinkage shall not exceed the national average of 2.2%. Memorandum of Objects and Reasons The principal objective of the Bill is to introduce necessary reforms in that strengthen and stabilize the cereals sub-sector, facilitate industry growth, promote food security in the country and that are in harmony with prevailing policy environment. The Bill repeals and replaces the National

text: the Bill is to introduce necessary reforms in that strengthen and stabilize the cereals sub-sector, facilitate industry growth, promote food security in the country and that are in harmony with prevailing policy environment. The Bill repeals and replaces the National Cereals and Produce Board Act with the National Grain Corporation Act. It provides for the powers, objects and functions of the National Grain Corporation in line with liberalization and commercialization policies. The Bill also establishes a Grain Development Fund for purposes of sustainability and stabilization of the Cereals Sub-sector. The Bill also provides for the Management of the affairs of the Corporation and other related matters. Part I provides for the short title of the proposed Act and its Commencement. Terms relevant to the Act are defined. Part II provides for the establishment, objects and powers of the Corporation as a body corporate with perpetual succession, common seal and capable of suing and being sued. The Bill provides for the functions of the Corporation which includes undertaking all aspects of grain trading, being the principle agent of Government for management of the strategic reserve and famine relief stocks, advising the Minister on national food reserve status and any desirable stabilization and government intervention measures in the grain market.
